title: Boltzmann Constant, Root Mean Square Speed and Heat Capacities
topicTitle: Boltzmann constant, root mean square speed
notes: **Boltzmann constant:** $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K. It connects microscopic and macroscopic thermodynamics. Named after Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906).
**RMS speed:** $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$, where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. At STP (273 K), $v_{rms}$ for air is about 479 m/s. At 300 K, about 484 m/s. Lighter gases move faster on average.
**Most probable speed:** $v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M}$. This is the speed at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks. At 300 K for air: $v_p \approx 364$ m/s. At 300 K for Hâ‚‚: $v_p \approx 1650$ m/s.
**Mean speed:** $v_{mean} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$. The average of all molecular speeds. At 300 K for air: $v_{mean} \approx 464$ m/s. At 300 K for Hâ‚‚: $v_{mean} \approx 1760$ m/s.

**Heat capacities - monatomic gases:** $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$. The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V = 5/3 \approx 1.67$. Monatomic gases (He, Ne, Ar) only have translational degrees of freedom.

**Heat capacities - diatomic gases:** $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$ at ordinary temperatures ($\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$). Includes 3 translational + 2 rotational DOF. At high temperature, vibration adds more, so $C_V \rightarrow 4R$, $C_P \rightarrow 5R$, $\gamma \rightarrow 9/7 \approx 1.29$.

**Dulong-Petit law for solids:** Molar heat capacity of most solid elements at room temperature $\approx 3R \approx 25$ J/(molÂ·K). This comes from 3 quadratic degrees of freedom per atom (one for each spatial axis), each contributing $R$ per mole of atoms.

**Why heat capacities differ:** The ratio $C_P/C_V = \gamma$ matters for adiabatic processes ($PV^\gamma = \text{const}$). This affects everything from engine cycles to atmospheric science. $\gamma \approx 1.4$ for air is crucial in meteorology.

**Experimental verification:** Heat capacities were measured by Regnault and others in the 19th century. The agreement with kinetic theory predictions was one of the great successes of molecular physics.
**Units:** $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K. $C_P, C_V$ have units J/(molÂ·K). Gas constant R has the same units.
**Connection to energy:** Each degree of freedom contributes $\frac{1}{2}R$ per mole or $\frac{1}{2}k_B$ per molecule. 3 translational DOF $ightarrow 3 \times \frac{1}{2}R = \frac{3}{2}R$ for $C_V$
confusion: The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is NOT always 5/3 or 7/5. It depends on temperature and molecular structure. At very high temperatures, vibrational modes activate, changing $\gamma$.
The formula $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$ applies ONLY to monatomic ideal gases. For diatomic or polyatomic gases, rotational (and sometimes vibrational) modes contribute.

Dulong's law ($C \approx 3R$) for solids works well at room temperature but fails at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze out degrees of freedom). Einstein and Debye developed low-temperature models.
The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ is NOT the same as the gas constant R. $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K per molecule. R = 8.314 J/(molÂ·K) per mole. $R = N_A k_B$.

Most probable speed is NOT the average speed. For the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: $v_p \cdot \sqrt{2} < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$. The order is always $v_p < v_{mean} < v_{rms}$ at the same temperature.
practice: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules (Nâ‚‚, M = 0.028 kg/mol) at 350 K. Solution: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3 \times 8.314 \times 350 / 0.028} = \sqrt{3471.8 / 0.028} = \sqrt{123,993} = 352$ m/s.

Find the most probable speed of helium atoms (He, M = 0.004 kg/mol) at 400 K. Solution: $v_p = \sqrt{2RT/M} = \sqrt{2 \times 8.314 \times 400 / 0.004} = \sqrt{6651.2 / 0.004} = \sqrt{1662800} = 1290$ m/s.

Calculate the mean speed of oxygen molecules (Oâ‚‚, M = 0.032 kg/mol) at 273 K. Solution: $v_{mean} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M} = \sqrt{8 \times 8.314 \times 273 / (\pi \times 0.032)} = \sqrt{18136 / 0.1005} = \sqrt{180,458} = 425$ m/s.

If the rms speed of helium at 300 K is 1250 m/s, what is the rms speed at 600 K? Solution: $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$. $v_{rms}(600) = v_{rms}(300) \times \sqrt{600/300} = 1250 \times \sqrt{2} = 1768$ m/s.
A container has 1 mol of gas at 300 K. What is the total internal energy for (a) monatomic gas? Solution: $U = \frac{3}{2}nRT = \frac{3}{2} \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 300 = 3741$ J.
Find the heat capacity ratio $\gamma$ for a diatomic gas at room temperature. Solution: $\gamma = C_P/C_V = (7/2R)/(5/2R) = 7/5 = 1.4$.
universalFacts: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution was first derived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1860 and later generalized by Ludwig Boltzmann. It describes the distribution of speeds in an ideal gas and is one of the most important results of kinetic theory.

At 300 K, the three speed measures for nitrogen (M=28 g/mol) are: most probable $v_p \approx 422$ m/s, mean speed $v_{mean} \approx 477$ m/s, and rms speed $v_{rms} \approx 517$ m/s. The ratios are always $v_p : v_{mean} : v_{rms} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{3} \approx 1.414 : 1.596 : 1.732$.

The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ was first introduced by Max Planck in his derivation of the blackbody radiation formula (1900). He used it to connect the energy of oscillators to temperature: $E = k_BT$.

Dulong and Petit's law ($C \approx 3R$ for solids) was discovered in 1819. It took nearly 150 years to understand why it works - the kinetic theory's 3 degrees of freedom per atom (1859-1870s) provided the explanation.

The ratio $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ determines whether sound speed is faster in an adiabatic process: $v_{sound} = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$. For air ($\gamma \approx 1.4$), $v_{sound} \approx 343$ m/s at 300 K. For helium ($\gamma = 5/3 \approx 1.67$), $v_{sound} \approx 965$ m/s at 300 K.
summary: The Boltzmann constant k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the bridge between microscopic molecular behaviour and macroscopic thermodynamics, and it sets the energy scale of a single molecule. Three characteristic molecular speeds follow from it, all proportional to √(T/M): the root-mean-square speed v_rms = √(3RT/M) ≈ 479 m/s for air at 273 K, the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT/M) at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks, and the mean speed v_mean = √(8RT/πM), with v_p < v_mean < v_rms always. Lighter molecules move faster, so hydrogen at roughly 1650 to 1760 m/s greatly outpaces air. Molecular heat capacities follow the same counting argument: a monatomic gas has only translational freedom, giving C_V = 3R/2, C_P = 5R/2 and γ = 5/3, while an ordinary diatomic gas adds two rotational degrees of freedom to give C_V = 5R/2, C_P = 7R/2 and γ = 7/5. At high temperatures vibration activates and γ falls towards 9/7, and for solids the Dulong-Petit law gives a molar heat capacity of about 3R ≈ 25 J/(mol·K).
importantConcepts: Boltzmann constant k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, linking the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of a gas.
Root-mean-square speed v_rms = √(3RT/M), about 479 m/s for air at 273 K and 484 m/s at 300 K.
Most probable speed v_p = √(2RT/M), the speed at which the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution peaks.
Mean speed v_mean = √(8RT/πM), the average over all molecular speeds, always ordered v_p < v_mean < v_rms.
Monatomic heat capacities C_V = 3R/2 and C_P = 5R/2 with γ = 5/3, from three translational degrees of freedom only.
Diatomic heat capacities C_V = 5R/2 and C_P = 7R/2 with γ = 7/5 at ordinary temperatures, from three translational plus two rotational degrees of freedom.
importantStatements: The Boltzmann constant is k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
The root-mean-square speed of a gas is v_rms = √(3RT/M), so lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature.
The most probable speed is v_p = √(2RT/M) and the mean speed is v_mean = √(8RT/πM).
For a monatomic ideal gas C_V = 3R/2, C_P = 5R/2 and γ = 5/3.
The Dulong-Petit law gives a molar heat capacity of about 3R ≈ 25 J/(mol·K) for most solid elements at room temperature.
importantTasks: Calculate the root-mean-square, most probable or mean speed of a gas from its molar mass and temperature.
Rank the three characteristic speeds of a gas and justify the ordering.
Determine γ and the molar heat capacities of a monatomic or diatomic gas from its degrees of freedom.
Compare the speeds of two different gases at the same temperature and explain the difference in terms of molar mass.
keyPoints: All three speeds scale as √(T/M), so doubling the temperature raises the speed by √2 and doubling the molar mass lowers it by √2.
The ordering v_p < v_mean < v_rms holds for every gas and is worth memorising as a single line.
C_V = 3R/2 is valid only for monatomic gases; diatomic gases add two rotational degrees of freedom.
γ is not a constant of nature: it is 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for ordinary diatomic, and falls towards 9/7 when vibration is excited at high temperature.
Hydrogen molecules move roughly three to four times faster than nitrogen at the same temperature because their molar mass is so much smaller.
specialNotes: The ratio γ = C_P/C_V is not always 5/3 or 7/5: it depends on temperature and molecular structure, and falls towards 9/7 when vibrational modes are excited at high temperature.
C_V = 3R/2 applies only to monatomic ideal gases; diatomic and polyatomic gases gain rotational and sometimes vibrational contributions.
For a diatomic gas at very high temperature the rotational modes are fully excited and C_V approaches 4R while C_P approaches 5R.
The three speeds are not interchangeable: v_p is where the distribution peaks, v_mean is the plain average, and v_rms is the square-root-mean-square, which is the largest of the three.
Molar mass must be in kg/mol for the speed formulas to give metres per second, so use 0.028 for nitrogen and 0.004 for helium.
examShortTricks: All three speed formulas differ only in the numerator, 2, 8/π and 3, so once you know v_p the others are quick multiples.
Convert molar mass to kg/mol before substituting; using 28 instead of 0.028 for nitrogen makes the answer wrong by a factor of √1000.
Read the question carefully for which speed is wanted, since v_rms, v_p and v_mean give visibly different numbers for the same gas.
Count degrees of freedom to fix γ: 3 for monatomic giving 5/3, 5 for diatomic giving 7/5.
examNotes: A three mark numerical on the root-mean-square speed of a named gas at a stated temperature is one of the most common questions in this unit.
Questions asking for the most probable or mean speed, or for a comparison of two gases, appear regularly.
One mark recall asks for the value of the Boltzmann constant and its role as the microscopic link.
Heat capacity ratios for monatomic and diatomic gases are a standard two or three mark item.
